title: Arignar Anna's Historic Public Pledge: 'Three Measures the Goal, One Measure Sure!' — 1967
summary: During the momentous 1967 elections, critics attacked Anna's visionary rice pledge as mathematically impossible. In Yojana and public rallies, Anna clarified with profound administrative realism: 'Three measures is our socialist goal; one measure for one rupee is our immediate guarantee!'
keywords: Arignar Anna's Historic Public Pledge: 'Three Measures the Goal, One Measure Sure!' — 1967
full_text:
In early 1967, Tamil Nadu was gripped by severe food shortages and spiraling grain prices. The working poor stood in serpentine ration queues for hours.

Against this backdrop, C.N. Annadurai launched his historic campaign. Across every public meeting, banner, and manifesto, the slogan echoed: "ரூபாய்க்கு மூன்று படி லட்சியம்; ஒரு படி நிச்சயம்!" (Three measures of rice for a rupee is our ultimate ideal; one measure is our immediate guarantee!).

Skeptical economists and rival political leaders took to the press, mocking the pledge as utopian fantasy. "How can any treasury finance such madness?" wrote opposing editorials.

In a comprehensive interview published in *Yojana* (the official journal of the Planning Commission of India in March 1967), Anna was questioned directly on the fiscal arithmetic of his promise.

Anna responded with calm political clarity:
"A leader who only promises what is already comfortably achievable has no ambition for his people. But a leader who promises castles in the sky without ground reality is a deceiver. We have done neither. Three measures for a rupee represents our moral economic target—a society where no child sleeps hungry. One measure for one rupee is our ironclad administrative contract."

When Anna assumed office as Chief Minister on March 6, 1967, his very first executive announcement launched the historic One-Rupee-a-Measure Rice Scheme in Chennai and Coimbatore, proving that political commitment can overcome administrative inertia.
